d: The back of a saddle seat
ety: From Middle English cantle, cantel, from Old Northern French cantel, Old French chantel (Modern French chanteau, Bourguignon chainteâ), from Medieval Latin cantellus, diminutive of Latin cantus (“corner”). Compare cant (Etymology 3). Kroonen instead connects this term with Dutch kant (“side; edge”) and German Kanz (“mane, upper part of the neck”), deriving them from a Proto-Germanic *kantaz (“side
s: He recognised a horse when he saw one, and could do more than fill a cantle.

d: Force into some kind of situation, condition, or course of action
ety: The verb is borrowed from French embrouiller (“to entangle”), from em- (a variant of en- (prefix meaning ‘in; into’)) + brouiller (“to confuse, mix up”) (ultimately from Vulgar Latin *brodiculāre, from *brodicāre, from Late Latin brodium (“broth, stew; mixture”), from Frankish *broþ (“broth”), from Proto-Germanic *bruþą (“stock, broth”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewh₁- (“to boil; to brew”)). Th
s: Avoid him. He will embroil you in his fights.

d: A dissolute person; usually a man who is morally unrestrained
ety: From Latin libertinus (“a freedman, prop. adj., of or belonging to the condition of a freedman”), from libertus (“a freedman”), from liber (“free”); see liberal, liberate.
s: So the truth of the matter is that a libertine in love, if indeed a libertine can be in love, becomes from that moment in less of a hurry to enjoy the pleasures of the flesh.

d: The property of excessive fatness
ety: From Old French corpulence, from Latin corpulentia.
s: Corpulence is a beauty: girls are fattened to a vast bulk by drenches of curds and cream thickened with flour, and are duly disciplined when they refuse.

d: An abject coward
ety: From Middle French poltron, from Italian poltrone.
s: You damned poltroon, you never tried them!

d: The right or chance to choose
ety: From the expression I'd rather (“I would prefer to”), often pronounced "I druther" in some dialects.
s: If I had my "druthers," I'd screw a chimpanzee. Call it, pointless.

d: Lose confidence or hope; become dejected
ety: From Latin dēspondeō (“give up, abandon”), from dē (“from”) + spondeō (“promise”).
s: Yet still despond not, but proceed Along the path where fate may lead.

d: A Russian carriage pulled by three horses abreast
ety: From Russian тро́йка (trójka, “a group of three”).
s: Travelling part of the way by rail and the remainder by troika, he reached Orenburg shortly before Christmas.

d: Of or occurring every seven days
ety: From Latin hebdomadālis. According to The Poly-Olbion Project, coined by John Selden in 1612.
s: The wits and humourists, the distinguished worthies of the town or village, the apothecary, the attorney, even the curate himself, did not disdain to partake of this hebdomadal festivity.

d: An inspiring symbol or ideal that serves as a rallying point in a struggle
ety: From Old French oriflambe, oriflamme, from Medieval Latin auriflamma (“golden flame”), from Latin aurum (“gold”) + flamma (“flame”).
s: And be your oriflamme to-day the helmet of Navarre.

d: Intense and continuous artillery fire
ety: Borrowed from Middle French canonnade, a modification of Italian cannonata replacing the suffix -ata with equivalent -ade; by surface analysis, cannon + -ade.
s: A furious cannonade was kept up from the whole circle of batteries on the devoted town.

d: Abounding in or given to pompous or aphoristic moralizing
ety: From Latin sententiōsus, from sententia (“opinion, purpose”).
s: His sententious remarks quickly bored the audience.

d: Audacious (even arrogant) behavior that you have no right to
ety: From late 17th century French effronterie, from effronté (“shameless, insolent”), from Old French esfronté, from Vulgar Latin *exfrontātus. Compare Latin effrōns (“barefaced”), from the prefix ex- (“from”) + frōns (“forehead”) (English: front). By surface analysis, ef- + front + -er + -y.
s: Any refusal to salute the president shall be counted as an effrontery.

d: Make unwanted and intrusive comments
ety: From Yiddish קיבעצן (kibetsn), cognate to German kiebitzen (“to look on”), from German Kiebitz (“lapwing”), from Middle High German gibiz (“plover”), imitative of its cry. Compare peewit.
s: Quit kibitzing! You're giving away my hand!

d: The state of something that is fully realized; actuality as opposed to potentiality
ety: From Late Latin entelechia, from Ancient Greek ἐντελέχεια (entelékheia), coined by Aristotle from ἐντελής (entelḗs, “complete, finished, perfect”) (from τέλος (télos, “end, fruition, accomplishment”)) + ἔχω (ékhō, “to have”).
s: But while these forces of chance work both in organic and in inorganic nature, there is an additional principle in organic (living) nature: an organizing principle or entelechie.

d: Make a rattling sound
ety: Apparently imitative, probably under influence of break + rattle.
s: Him too I hate, the same as I hate these brainless budding trees, these brattling birds.

d: A tremulous sound
ety: From Middle English quaveren, frequentative form of quaven, cwavien (“to tremble”), equivalent to quave + -er. Cognate with Low German quabbeln (“to quiver”), German quabbeln, quappeln (“to quiver”). More at quave, quab, quiver.
s: The crotchets and quavers are dancing up and down the stave like little black boys on a fence.

d: The abode of Satan and the forces of evil; where sinners suffer eternal punishment
ety: From Middle English perdicioun, from Old French perdiciun, from Late Latin perditio, from Latin perdo (“to destroy, to lose”).
s: Their decision to buy stocks just before the crisis led to their perdition.

d: A small rounded boat made of hides stretched over a wicker frame; still used in some parts of Great Britain
ety: Of Celtic origin; related to Welsh corwg, Irish curach (“boat”) and Cornish gorhel (“ship”), from Proto-Celtic *kurukos (“boat”).
s: The White Hart, overlooking the bridge, has a bar named after the coracles that may still be seen on this part of the Teifi.

d: A small bagpipe formerly popular in France
ety: From both of the following: * Late Middle English musette (“type of bagpipe”), from Middle French musette, Old French musette (“type of bagpipe”) (modern French musette), from muse (“bagpipe”) + -ette (diminutive suffix). Muse is derived from muser (“to play the bagpipe; (figuratively) to flatter”), perhaps from musel (“muzzle (protruding part of an animal’s head)”) (alluding to a bagpipe player p
s: The young gentleman had a musette over his shoulder.

d: A governor of a province in ancient Persia
ety: From Middle English satrape, from Latin satrapēs (“governor”), from Ancient Greek σατράπης (satrápēs), from Old Median *xšaθrapāvan (literally “kingdom-protector”), which is cognate with Old Persian 𐎧𐏁𐏂𐎱𐎠𐎺𐎠 (xšaçapāvā); see there for more.
s: Eunuchs were chiefly employed in the harems of the king, and his satraps.

d: Worn and broken down by hard use
ety: From Middle English wo-bigon, wo-begon (“(adjective) deeply affected by woe, distressed, sorrowful, wretched; affected by physical impairment or pain; tired, weary; abominable, cursed; (noun) unfortunate person, wretch”), from wo (“distress, misery, woe; physical pain or suffering; etc.”) + bigon (the past participle form of bigon (“of a state: to come upon or overtake (someone), beset, overwhelm,
s: I now went down to have a look at the "port." It was the most woebegone excavation, full of mud and fishy refuse, you ever saw.

d: A child who spends most of his time in the streets especially in slum areas
ety: From gutter + snipe.
s: Never lose a chance: it doesnt come everyday. I shall make a duchess of this draggletailed guttersnipe.

d: Not straightforward or candid; giving a false appearance of frankness
ety: From dis- + ingenuous.
s: I am not so vain as to think these Remarks free from faults, nor so disingenuous as not to confess them:

d: Try to stir up public opinion
ety: From Middle English fomenten, a borrowing from Old French fomenter, from Late Latin fōmentāre, from Latin fōmentum (“lotion”), from fovēre (“heat, cherish”).
s: Foreign governments have tried to foment unrest.

d: A metal helmet worn by common soldiers in the 16th century
ety: From Middle French morion, from, Spanish morrión, from morra (“upper part of the head”), from morro (“muzzle, snout”), from Vulgar Latin *murrum (“muzzle, snout”). Related to moraine (“an amassment of rocks on a glacier”).
s: The morion is a kind of open helmet, without visor or bever, somewhat resembling a hat; it was commonly worn by the harqubussiers and musqueteers.

d: A desk used for writing
ety: From French escritoire, from escrire (“to write”) (obsolete forms of écritoire and écrire, respectively) + -oire (“a tool or object”). Doublet of scriptorium.
s: Rosemary sat at her Public Works Department escritoire, in a sea of fed cats, and tried to write a letter to Vythilingam.

d: Moving and bending with ease
ety: From Middle English lithsum, equivalent to lithe + -some. Doublet of lithesome.
s: A brig you see, sir, is much more laboursome in a gale of wind. A Schooner is much lissomer built.

d: A large entrance or reception room or area
ety: From Middle French antichambre, with remodelling after ante- and chamber. By surface analysis, ante- + chamber.
s: Gun, escort them to the antechamber until the Avatar's arrival.

d: Of size and dignity suggestive of a statue
ety: Unadapted borrowing from French statuesque. By surface analysis, statu(e) + -esque.
s: Christy Turlington is a statuesque supermodel famous for her fashion ads.

d: Living quarters reserved for wives and concubines and female relatives in a Muslim household
ety: From Italian serraglio, from Vulgar Latin *serrāculum, from a late form of Latin serāre (“lock up, close”), from sera (“lock, bolt”). The Italian word was used (because of phonetic similarity) to translate Turkish saray (“palace”). Compare serai, serail.
s: At these words he started up, and beheld—not his Sophia—no, nor a Circassian maid richly and elegantly attired for the grand Signior's seraglio.

d: A new convert being taught the principles of Christianity by a catechist
ety: From Middle English cathecumynys pl, from Middle French cathecumin (modern French catéchumène) or Ecclesiastical Latin catēchūmenus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κατηχούμενος (katēkhoúmenos, “being instructed”), present participle passive of κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “sound through, instruct orally, catechise”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound”).
s: Here in this room an old man had killed and boiled a catechumen, had committed sodomy with a rat, had discussed a rodent nunhood with V., a future saint – depending which story you listened to.

d: Too numerous to be counted
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin multitūdin- (the oblique stem of multitūdō (“great number (of people), multitude”)) + English -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, denoting the presence of a quality in any degree (typically an abundance)). Multitūdō is derived from multus (“many; much”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mel- (“to be late; to worry”)) + -tūdō (suffix forming abstract nouns d
s: The lesser fowls / Flock multitudinous in heaven, and fly / Before the Eagle's coming.

d: Thunderous verbal attack
s: The senator was prone to diatribes which could go on for more than an hour.

d: Given or giving freely
ety: Inherited from Middle English bountevous, from Old French bontios; by surface analysis, bounty + ous.
s: The house came with a bounteous yard.

d: A primitive wind instrument consisting of several parallel pipes bound together
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin sȳrinx (“reed; reed pipe, panpipes”), from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx, “panpipes; pipe-shaped object”), from Pre-Greek. Doublet of syringe. The plural form syringes is a learned borrowing from Latin sȳringes.
s: The myelin around the syrinx shows changes similar to edematous white matter, probably due to tearing of the tissues and transudation of serous fluid into them.

d: A light plain-weave or twill-weave silk or silklike fabric (usually with a printed design)
ety: Borrowed from French foulard.
s: A lot of foulard tie bulged out and was rain-spotted above his crossed lapels.

d: Bending the head or body or knee as a sign of reverence or submission or shame or greeting
ety: From Middle English obeisaunce (“obedience, obeisance”), from Old French obeïssance, derived from obeïssant (“obedient”), participle of obeïr (“to obey”), from Latin oboediō, obēdiō; ob- (“to, for”) + audiō (“to hear”). Cognate with obedience.
s: In there stepped a stately raven of the saintly days of yore; / Not the least obeisance made he; not a minute stopped or stayed he;

d: Pleasant and beneficial in nature or influence
ety: From benign + -ant, on the model of malignant.
s: General Peckem roused himself after a moment with an unctuous and benignant smile.

d: Elegant and stylish
ety: From vogue + -ish.
s: It’s hard to say the precise moment when CBD, the voguish cannabis derivative, went from being a fidget spinner alternative for stoners to a mainstream panacea.
